name: Gadang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Jungraithmayr, Herrmann. 2006. Apophony in the verbal system of Gadang. Studies in African Linguistics 35 (Supplement 11: West African Linguistics: Papers in honor of Russell G. Schuh, ed. Paul Newman & Larry M. Hyman): 134-144. DOI 10.32473/sal.v35i0.107320
catalog_locator: sec. 3.1 'Vowels and Tones', pp. 135-136; file, pages 2-3 read
catalog_quote: Gadang is a 7-vowel language comprising the basic 5 vowels i, e, a, o, u, plus 2 central vowels, high ə and low ʌ. This is in full conformity with its immediate eastern neighbour, Sarwa, as well as with its southern relative, Sibine (Sumray). As to the tonal structure, Gadang distinguishes three level tones, high á, mid (a or ā) and low à, and three tonal glides, high-low (â, áà), high-mid (áā), and mid-high (aá or āá). Both vowels and tones are heavily involved in the formation of the verbal aspect stems. Ninety-three of the 165 verbs do not display ablaut, but distinguish their aspect stems by tone ("abton") and the appropriate suffixes. That is to say, only 72, i.e., less than half of our sample, exhibit some sort of apophony.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gadang is described as a lexical/grammatical tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low) and three contour tones (HL, HM, MH); tone alone distinguishes perfective from imperfective in more than half of the verbs. The only accessible first-hand description says nothing whatever about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none; tone inventory given without minimal pairs; suffix -gA copies the tone of the perfective base, and tone/length of the imperfective suffix -a/-aa 'vary considerably' with the shape of the base
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns tone on verb stems and aspect stems from a 165-verb sample recorded in March 1973 at Bousso (informant M. Kalamsa Djom). No stress domain (word vs phrase) is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Same language as Glottolog gada1262 / ISO gdk (Gadang, Gadango; Jungraithmayr's autonym gàdàŋ), spoken in villages around Bousso on the Chari (Taouan, Gadang Kiao, Djaména, Morio, Balo, Gadang, Gadang-Gougouri, Gadang Haddad Daudi, Madjoum). All first-hand data come from one informant, M. Kalamsa Djom, recorded by Jungraithmayr at Bousso in March 1973; no dialects are named. Glottolog places it in East Chadic A.1 (Sumray group); Wikipedia's 'Miltu subgroup' label follows Barreteau & Newman 1978 / Ethnologue.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent/intonation: no hits; sec. 3.1 read on the page scan). Sec. 3.1 'Vowels and Tones' (pp. 135-136) gives 7 vowels and states Gadang has three level tones (H, M, L) and three glides (HL, HM, MH); tone ('abton') and ablaut mark the perfective/imperfective opposition. First-hand data: 165 verbs recorded March 1973 at Bousso from M. Kalamsa Djom; the author states this is the first information on Gadang ever published.

sources.note: Phonology is of Boor, not Gadang. Source of the Vanderkooi 1990 and Faris & Ndotar 1994 records.
